title: Disclosed AI on my Steam idle game. Here's what reviews and refunds looked like in week one
author: drive_wave
selftext:
*(TL;DR at the end)*

Long time lurker, figured this sub might find some actual numbers useful.

Quick background, I've been in games for 12+ years. Mostly mobile and F2P (5M+ downloads across my titles), a stint in AAA, and these days I make my own PC games and consult on the side.

Last week I launched Coin Harvest, a little desktop widget idle where you run a coin pusher in the corner of your screen. The store page has an AI disclosure for the store page art and some in-game render assets.

I don't use AI that heavily, mostly for boring stuff and for adding detail in places where it actually makes the game nicer to look at. The reason it works for me is the 12 years before it. Gamedev is mostly knowing what not to do, and that's exactly what AI can't tell you. I know what bad output looks like and I catch most problems before they ever reach the game. Not all of them, as the rest of this post shows. I disclosed it because that's the rule and I didn't want to play games with it.

Here's how the first week went.

**Numbers**

* About 4,500 copies in the first 36 hours, \~6,900 now. CCU peaked around 600 and it's been sitting at 400-500 since
* Refunds are at 11% overall, but that number hides a lot. US and Japan are at 5-6%, UK 8%. China, Korea and CIS are almost 3x that
* Median playtime is about 2.5 hours four days in, average is 6. 56% of players are already past the 2 hour refund window, 17% past 10 hours. For a widget some of that is just the window being left open, but it's not what you'd expect from a game that's "beaten in 30 minutes"
* Review score was 83% on launch day. Three days later it was 55%, Mixed
* And that 55% is just 49 reviews. For \~6,900 copies. That's 1 review per 140 copies, when the usual rule of thumb is somewhere around 1 per 60
* The game got some attention on X on day three. Refunds for people who bought that day went from 10% to 16%, and the next day only 3 of 13 new reviews were positive. Before and after that it was hovering around 60%

**What the bad reviews actually said**

I read all of them. Honestly a lot of it was fair.

Time warp in the crystal shop could be chained to blow through realms in minutes. Coins could get stuck where the arm couldn't reach and mess up the coin cap. Upgrades didn't feel like they did much. Realms felt samey. There was a transparency mode bug, no cloud saves at launch, some performance issues. I've fixed a bunch of that in 1.0.3 through 1.0.8 and the rest is on the list.

Then there were the ones with no gameplay in them at all. "AI slop", "AI garbage", one guy who reviewed it and then opened a forum thread starting with "Just saw on X".

The ones that stuck with me were in between. Someone finds a real problem and then explains it with AI. Late game balance is off, so "AI made it, nobody tested it". Time warp is broken, so "dev never played it". No auto-clicker protection, so "vibe-coded, zero knowledge of game development". The bug was real. The reason they gave for it wasn't. And even after you fix it, the review still reads like it's about you, not the game.

**What I think is going on**

The label doesn't create the flaws, it kills the tolerance. Stuff that would get a "small indie, they'll patch it" on another game gets treated as proof here. The 24h and 7 day achievements are pretty normal for widget idlers and nobody blinked at them in my other games. On this one they were the main thing people went after.

A lot of reviews also judged it as something it isn't. It's a desktop toy that sits in the corner while you work, not a deep incremental you sit and optimize. That's spelled out on the store page, and the free demo shows exactly what it is. It still kept getting measured against Melvor and Cell to Singularity, and called "not deep enough" or "beaten in 30 minutes". When people are already looking for a reason, a genre they didn't sign up for becomes one more.

A lot of the harshest reviews have 10 to 24 hours on record. For a widget idle that's normal, it's made to sit open. But it's hard to square "beaten in 30 minutes" or "no content" with 20 hours played, and a few of them kept playing well after posting the review. The game is $3.99, $3.19 at launch. I'm not saying cheap means it's above criticism, but the bar it got judged by didn't match the price or the genre.

I still think the angry crowd is small. Refunds in the big markets are low and people are still playing. But someone who's enjoying a small idle game in the background almost never writes a review, and someone who's mad about the label always does. When 49 people set the score for 7,000 players, that's all it takes.

Once people know AI was involved, everything starts looking like AI. Fonts, colors, a UI layout, things that had nothing to do with it. And honestly, the parts that did use AI would have been easy to polish until nobody could tell. I left them as they were and disclosed it, because hiding it felt worse than taking the hit. After this week I understand why a lot of devs make the other choice.

What actually worries me is the incentive. Pretty much everyone is using AI somewhere in their pipeline now, and a solo dev who refuses to is just competing with one hand tied. So if being honest about it costs this much, the obvious move is to not disclose, or wait until reviews settle. Some people already do that, and the ones who are good at hiding it are usually the good devs. Nobody wins there, including people who actually want to avoid AI games.

**What I'd do differently**

* Make the core loop feel better before launch. If people are less forgiving, polish matters more
* Don't argue with reviewers, on Steam or anywhere else. One reply, say what you fixed, move on. I didn't do this at first and it made everything worse
* Watch refunds per region from day one. Bad localization showed up there way before it showed up in reviews

Happy to answer questions or dig into more numbers if anyone's curious.

[https://store.steampowered.com/app/4381180/Coin\_Harvest/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4381180/Coin_Harvest/)

**TL;DR** Solo dev, disclosed AI on a small $4 widget idle. Score went from 83% to 55% in three days off just 49 reviews across \~6,900 copies. A lot of the criticism was fair and got patched, but the AI label wiped out the usual tolerance an indie gets, and the day it blew up on X refunds jumped from 10% to 16%. Honest disclosure is getting punished hard enough that hiding it is starting to look like the rational move, and that's bad for everyone.

comments.author: tickscribe
comments.body:
JM2C:  
  
I am also a little bit worried. The whole "No AI" stuff is getting more and more toxic. Of course, pure AI Slop and games just build by reverse engineering existing games, is nothing somebody want's to have. But I am also using AI where it makes sense to me (15+ years of software development and systems engineering is a solid basis for this). GitHub Copilot automcomplete in VSCode? Of course, it is a great tool to speed up programming. Writing test cases and unit tests for my code? Hell yeah, every developer hates this. Translations? Sure thing, AI is better in translating text than humans and nobody wants to have bad translations.

In my current game, I have a single wallpaper for the start screen which is the only thing you could call "AI slop". I am not a designer, I am in a early alpha phase, I don't want to spend money for a matching wallpaper in that early stage. But as soon as I am honest and write down the "AI disclosure", the whole game is tagged as "AI slop", I am called "talentless" and I should "never touch any game development ever".... 

I know, for all the groups on Reddit, Steam and Itchio, AI slop is a real problem and danger. But on the other side, the whole community is getting more and more toxic on that topic.

What bothers me the most, that most of the "AI slop" posters do not even understand the difference between AI tools and AI supported features, and real GenAI. Nowadays, NOBODY is efficiently working without AI support, otherwise you will become unproductive and slow in professional environments. Of course you could still do all the work manually, but before AI there was no "Stackoverflow disclosure" for copy&paste software built from Stackoverflow snippets.

comments.author: AsparagusOk8818
comments.body:
The social risk is that if your game is popular, your life could literally be ruined. Someone posts on a social media platform about it; an influencer picks it up, and suddenly millions of people are not talking about the game but are talking about how you are a liar and a fraud (from their perspective). And then the whole negativity and drama machine spins into motion, and talking about you as a bad guy and posting thumbnails of you becomes its own commodity. Shitting on you becomes a lucrative currency.

There are entire ecosystems of the Internet that purely trade in that currency.

People will find your address, your email, your contact info, your employers, your family. They will endlessly harass, and the cycle of abuse doesn't stop for months after the initial viral drama because people keep stumbling into it and want to participate.

People will dig old skeletons out of your closet and will make some up for good measure. You will become the person who just has to deal with that for a long-ass time.

All because you didn't include a little disclosure on the game, and it became popular enough to be noticed and scrutinized.

There's probably not a whole lot of legal risk, but Steam could easily ban your account, and would do so if public pressure was sufficiently high. There's a non-zero risk of litigation from people who felt falsely advertised to, and they'd have a somewhat reasonable case since you violated the labelling rules.

replies.author: AsparagusOk8818
replies.body:
Sure, look at what happened to Lindsey Ellis. Look at what happened to the Marathon devs.

And yes, it is far worse than what the criminal justice system does, because of course it is; it's vigilante mob 'justice'.   


So that is what you are risking when you decide that you don't want to disclose because you're afraid of lost sales. A few dollars here or there at the mere risk of the Internet deciding you are the villain of the week and need to have your life destroyed.

comments.author: drive_wave
comments.body:
Mobile is one of the "perfected" areas of gaming and that's why its incredibly profitable and even just 1 game can make billions. It's not about uniqueness etc. It's down to a simple metric, is it fun to play. AI only made that process faster. Inventing novel concepts for an already perfected workflow is damn near impossible

As you said Coin Harvest is fun but not "exciting" and it shouldn't and does not try to be. Simply it's not designed to be exciting. It's designed to keep you company while you do your other things and sporadicly look at. I agree that it carries a mobile-esque design but  it just simply works. That's why its doing good on a wider perspective. It's getting bombed to shit on Steam because of anti-AI cynicism. CCU is still solid because it's a novel mechanic for Steam players. Tho I don't say it is perfect. Still has its flaws and anti-AI is making it 10x worse than it really is. 

It took me around 300h, which is around a month of work with all playtesting etc and it's a live game so will take a lot more time too. Yes getting a proto quick is nice but you still need a lot of gamedev knowledge to even get something like this. AI cut the tedious parts but still requires experience to make "good" games

replies.author: MeasIIDX
replies.body:
Specifically, I mentioned that the game looks fun but doesn't make me excited to play it for $3 which isn't a reflection on your non-exciting game by choice. Perhaps what I want to say is that nothing is driving me to give it a purchase because it's hard to differentiate it from other games vying for my attention in this genre.
 
There's nothing wrong with your intention of making this game and designing it this way, but you are trying to cut into a  "perfected" market. It suggests that your success is based on luck (which is part of success no doubt) but I'm a believer that luck can be mitigated by other factors and from a first impression your game does not make me a purchaser. 

I'm also working on two games using AI to develop as well with most of the assets from itch.io. One of them I've been working on since last November. I'm not unfamiliar to the level of effort that can be put in both with and without AI. It could be a different for me though because I didn't intend on selling the game because its more of a passion side project.

Best of luck!

comments.author: MessageSelfdestructs
comments.body:
I've worked as a 3D artist professionally for 15 years, and probably 25 years in total.  
So I'm known with 3D modeling and creating textures.  
Outside of that, as a hobby in my spare time, over the past decade or so I've worked a lot with 2D (pixel art and all that jazz).

So most of the assets for my game have been created by myself, though I've also trained an AI-model on my own 2D art from the past decade, which made me able to generate some of my enemies/characters in my games (which then also needed some refinement to not look AI-generated), though most of my characters (like the main characters and enemies) were created by myself.

comments.author: MessageSelfdestructs
comments.body:
Yeah, I think you're right about that, though there are also some very obvious tells that are easily masked (such as the UI, the use of the default font, imperfect 2D pixel art, sloppy animations, inconsistent alignment of objects, etc.) where you don't need to have industry experience.

But I'd say it really helps that I've been involved in creating art for computer games for at least 2 decades, and also that I'm kind of a perfectionist. So even when art isn't generated by AI, I'm incredibly nitpicky and spend a lot of time on polish. More so now when I'm working for myself, as previously when I worked for game companies, I of course had deadlines, and as such needed to prioritise what I could polish, or what I just needed to leave as-is.
